title: Isolation Levels & Anomalies
html:
Full isolation is expensive, so SQL defines four levels that trade correctness for concurrency. Each level forbids a different set of anomalies.

The anomalies

AnomalyWhat happensExample
Dirty readT2 reads data T1 has written but not committedT1 debits 200, T2 reads 800, T1 rolls back — T2 used a value that never existed
Non-repeatable readT1 reads a row twice and gets different values because T2 committed an update in betweenBalance 1000, then 800 in the same report
Phantom readT1 re-runs a range query and sees new/removed rows committed by T2COUNT(*) WHERE dept_id = 1 is 4, then 5
Lost updateT1 and T2 both read 1000, both write back their own result — one update disappearsTwo withdrawals of 100 leave 900 instead of 800
Write skewTwo transactions each check a condition, then write different rows, together breaking the ruleTwo on-call doctors each go off duty because “the other is on call”

The four standard levels

LevelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantomNotes
READ UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossibleRarely used; PostgreSQL treats it as Read Committed
READ COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossibleDefault in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle
REPEATABLE READNoNoPossible (standard) — prevented by snapshots in PostgreSQL/MySQLDefault in MySQL InnoDB
SERIALIZABLENoNoNoAs if transactions ran one at a time; may abort with serialization errors — retry

Seeing it: two sessions on one SQLite file

SQLite in WAL mode gives each reading transaction a snapshot (like Repeatable Read/Serializable) and allows one writer at a time. Two connections play two users:

Key point

Under READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL's default), B's third read would already return 800 — each statement sees the latest committed data. That's the non-repeatable read the level allows.

Preventing lost updates

Atomic update

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 — read-modify-write happens inside one statement. Best when possible.

Pessimistic lock

SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the row until commit, so the second transaction waits.

Optimistic check

UPDATE … SET balance = :new, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 1 AND version = :read_version — 0 rows updated means someone else won; retry.

Serializable

Let the database detect the conflict and abort one transaction; the app retries.

What isolation level would you use?

Usually the engine default (Read Committed in PostgreSQL/SQL Server/Oracle, Repeatable Read in MySQL) combined with atomic updates or SELECT … FOR UPDATE for read-modify-write. Use SERIALIZABLE for complex invariants spanning several rows (write skew) and be ready to retry on serialization failures.

What is a phantom read?

Re-running the same range query in one transaction returns a different set of rows because another transaction committed an insert or delete in that range. Non-repeatable reads are about changed values of existing rows; phantoms are about rows appearing or disappearing.
